document_metadata.title: Guideline Based Management of Primary Dysmenorrhea: A Clinical Flow Chart Guide

workflow_steps: 1. Initial Approach: Establish rapport & privacy, Detailed history, Menstrual history, Associated symptoms, Medication & family history, Physical examination, Identify red flags
2. Initial Evaluation: History & examination consistent with primary dysmenorrhea, No abnormal pelvic findings, Consider further evaluation if diagnosis is uncertain to exclude secondary causes
3. Diagnosis: Cyclic lower abdominal pain during menses, Begins shortly after menarche, No pelvic pathology, Normal pelvic exam, Normal investigations, Exclude secondary causes
4. Management & Follow-Up: Stepwise individualized treatment, Start with non-pharmacologic measures, Use pharmacologic therapy based on severity, Reassess & step up if needed, Follow-up in 3-6 months

conditions_registry.condition_name: Mild Primary Dysmenorrhea (Minimal impact on daily activities)

key_features: Cramping lower abdominal pain at onset of menses
Little or no interference with daily activities

initial_conservative: Non-Pharmacologic Measures: Education & reassurance, Heat therapy, Regular exercise, Adequate sleep, Stress reduction (yoga, relaxation), Dietary measures
specific_advanced: Second-Line / Adjunctive (If inadequate relief): NSAIDs (Ibuprofen, Mefenamic acid, Naproxen, Diclofenac) starting at onset or 1-2 days before menses
Third-Line Options (If persistent pain): Different NSAID agent or dose optimization, Add antispasmodic (e.g., Drotaverine), Magnesium supplement, Vitamin B1 / E
follow_up_monitoring: Assess pain relief, side effects & adherence
Return earlier if worsening or new symptoms

conditions_registry.condition_name: Moderate Primary Dysmenorrhea (Interferes with some activities)

key_features: Interferes with school, work or routine activities
May have nausea, vomiting, headache, diarrhoea, backache

initial_conservative: NSAIDs (First-line pharmacologic): Start early at onset or 1-2 days before menses
specific_advanced: Second-Line / Adjunctive (If inadequate relief): Switch/optimize NSAID, Add antispasmodic, Consider Tranexamic acid (if heavy bleeding), Magnesium / Vitamin B1 / E
Third-Line Options (If persistent pain): COCPs (cyclic or extended), Progestin-only pills, LNG-IUS, Lifestyle & stress management support

conditions_registry.condition_name: Severe Primary Dysmenorrhea (Marked impact / bed rest)

key_features: Marked interference with daily activities / school or work absenteeism
Associated symptoms prominent (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, headache, fatigue)

initial_conservative: NSAIDs (First-line): Adequate dose, early initiation for 2-3 days
Consider antiemetic if severe nausea / vomiting
specific_advanced: Second-Line / Adjunctive (If inadequate relief): Switch to another NSAID or higher dose, Add antispasmodic, Add tranexamic acid, Short course simple analgesic (paracetamol) as adjunct
Third-Line Options (Hormonal Therapy): COCPs (cyclic / extended), LNG-IUS, Progestin-only options (e.g., DMPA, implant), Consider GnRH agonist (rare; refractory cases under specialist care)
follow_up_monitoring: Assess pain relief, quality of life & side effects
Monitor BP (if on COCP), weight, mood
If inadequate relief, reassess for secondary causes

conditions_registry.condition_name: Refractory / Treatment Failure (No adequate relief despite optimal therapy)

key_features: Persistent pain despite optimal medical therapy (3-6 months)
Significant impact on quality of life

initial_conservative: Reassess: Confirm diagnosis, Review adherence, Assess severity & pattern, Rule out secondary causes (endometriosis, adenomyosis) if atypical features present
specific_advanced: Adjunctive Options: Optimize hormonal therapy, Add adjuncts (neuromodulators e.g. amitriptyline, gabapentin), Pelvic floor physical therapy, Psychological support / CBT
Specialist Referral: Gynecologist / pain specialist, Consider diagnostic laparoscopy (if suspicion of endometriosis), Multidisciplinary approach

clinical_best_practices: Start treatment early (1-2 days before or at onset of menses)
Use lowest effective dose for shortest duration
Individualize based on severity, preference, comorbidities & goals
Reassess regularly & step up if needed
Consider impact on quality of life & mental health
disclaimer: This chart is a guide only. Clinical judgment is essential. Early recognition and appropriate management improve outcomes in women.
